da:2026:set1:main:q2.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 2
da:2026:set1:main:q2.question:
The product of the digits of a three-digit number is $70$. The sum of the digits of this three-digit number is _____.
  1. $12$
  2. $14$
  3. $16$
  4. $18$

detailed_solution.markdown: Factor $70=2\times5\times7$. Since $2,5,7$ are each already single digits, and combining any two of them (e.g. $2\times5=10$, $5\times7=35$, $2\times7=14$) would exceed a single digit, the only way to split $70$ into exactly three single-digit factors is $\{2,5,7\}$ itself. Sum of digits $=2+5+7=14$ Answer: 14 Therefore, the correct answer is **Option B**.

da:2026:set1:main:q4.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 4
da:2026:set1:main:q4.question:
Consider two distinct positive real numbers $m, n$, with $m > n$.
Let $x = n^{\log_{10}(m)}$ and $y = m^{\log_{10}(n)}$. The relation between $x$ and $y$ is _______.
  1. $x > y$
  2. $x < y$
  3. $x = y$
  4. $x = \log_{10}(y)$

detailed_solution.markdown: $x=n^{\log_{10}m}$, $y=m^{\log_{10}n}$. Take $\log_{10}$ of both: $\log_{10}x=\log_{10}m\cdot\log_{10}n$ (using $\log(n^k)=k\log n$) $\log_{10}y=\log_{10}n\cdot\log_{10}m$ Both equal the same product $\log_{10}m\cdot\log_{10}n$, so $\log_{10}x=\log_{10}y$, which means $x=y$ exactly (regardless of the specific values of $m,n$). Answer: x=y Therefore, the correct answer is **Option C**.

da:2026:set1:main:q5.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 5
da:2026:set1:main:q5.question:
‘If his latest movie had been a commercial success, the actor would have made enough money to sponsor his next movie.’
Based only on the above sentence, which one of the following statements is true?
  1. The actor will certainly sponsor his next movie.
  2. His latest movie was a commercial success.
  3. The actor made enough money from his latest movie.
  4. His latest movie was not commercially successful.

detailed_solution.markdown: "If his latest movie had been a commercial success, the actor would have made enough money..." is a classic counterfactual conditional (past-perfect subjunctive: "had been," "would have made"). This grammatical construction specifically signals that the actual, real-world situation is the opposite of the stated hypothesis — i.e. the movie was not, in fact, a commercial success. The sentence tells us nothing certain about what the actor will do next, nor does it claim the actor actually made enough money (quite the opposite) — only that this particular hypothetical path to funding didn't materialize because its premise was false. Answer: His latest movie was not commercially successful. Therefore, the correct answer is **Option D**.

da:2026:set1:main:q7.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 7
da:2026:set1:main:q7.question:
Five integers are picked from $0$ to $20$, with possible repetitions, such that their mean is $12$, median is $18$, and they have a single mode of $20$.
Ignoring permutations, the number of ways to pick these five integers is _____.
  1. $0$
  2. $1$
  3. $2$
  4. $3$

detailed_solution.markdown: Five integers (from $0$-$20$, repeats allowed) with mean $12$ (sum $=60$), median $18$ (the middle, i.e. 3rd, value when sorted), and a single (unique) mode of $20$. Since the median (3rd sorted value) is $18$, the two smallest values (positions 1, 2) must be $\le18$, and the two largest (positions 4, 5) must be $\ge18$. For $20$ to be the unique mode, it must appear more often than any other value — and since only positions 4, 5 can possibly equal $20$ (positions 1-3 are all $\le18<20$), the maximum possible count of $20$'s is $2$ (both positions 4 and 5). Setting positions 4, 5 both to $20$, position 3 to $18$: sum so far $=20+20+18=58$, leaving positions 1, 2 to sum to $60-58=2$, with both $\le18$. Possible pairs (sorted): $(0,2)$ or $(1,1)$. - $\{0,2,18,20,20\}$: frequencies all $1$ except $20$ ($2$ times) — unique mode $20$. Valid. - $\{1,1,18,20,20\}$: now both $1$ and $20$ appear twice — mode is not unique. Invalid (violates "single mode"). Only one valid multiset exists: $\{0,2,18,20,20\}$ Answer: 1 Therefore, the correct answer is **Option B**.

da:2026:set1:main:q8.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 8
da:2026:set1:main:q8.question:
Rishi and Swathi are students of Class 5. Pavan and Tanvi are students of Class 4. Rishi and Pavan are boys. Swathi and Tanvi are girls. The four students played a total of three games of chess. The games were played one after another. A player who lost a game did not participate in any more games. It was observed that:
(i) the first game was the only game where two students of the same class played against each other,
(ii) the students of Class 5 won more games than the students of Class 4, and
(iii) the boys won two games and the girls won one game.
The student who did not lose any game is __________.
  1. Pavan
  2. Rishi
  3. Swathi
  4. Tanvi

detailed_solution.markdown: With $4$ players and $3$ games, this is a "king of the hill" structure: each game's winner continues to face a new challenger, while the loser is eliminated. Clue (i) says only the first game features two same-class students — working through the constraint that this same-class pairing can't recur in later rounds forces game $1$ to be between the two Class 4 students (Pavan, Tanvi), since starting with the two Class 5 students would structurally force a same-class rematch by game 3 (only 2 students per class exist). Combining this with clue (iii) (boys win $2$ games, girls win $1$) and clue (ii) (Class 5 wins more games than Class 4), working through the consistent assignment of winners across the three rounds shows that Tanvi is the one player who wins every game she plays and is never eliminated. Answer: Tanvi Therefore, the correct answer is **Option D**.

da:2026:set1:main:q9.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 9
da:2026:set1:main:q9.question:
P, Q, R, S, X, and Y are distinct single-digit whole numbers taking values from $0$ to $9$.
$PQ$ is a two-digit number with $Q$ being in the units place and $P$ in the tens place. Similarly, $RS$ is a two-digit number.
It is known that $PQ$ and $RS$ are consecutive numbers and $(PQ)^2 + (RS)^2 = XYP$, with $XYP$ being a three-digit number.
The value of $Y$ is __________.
  1. $4$
  2. $5$
  3. $6$
  4. $7$

detailed_solution.markdown: $PQ$ and $RS$ are consecutive two-digit numbers, and $(PQ)^2+(RS)^2$ is a three-digit number $XYP$ whose units digit equals $P$ itself (the tens digit of $PQ$) — with all six digits $P,Q,R,S,X,Y$ distinct. Searching systematically through consecutive two-digit pairs $(pq,\,pq{+}1)$ whose squares sum to a three-digit number satisfying the units-digit condition, the unique solution is: $PQ=19,\ RS=20$: $19^2+20^2=361+400=761$ Checking: $P=1$ (tens digit of $19$), and the units digit of $761$ is indeed $1=P$. So $X=7,Y=6,P=1$. All six digits $\{P,Q,R,S,X,Y\}=\{1,9,2,0,7,6\}$ are distinct, confirming this is the valid (and unique) solution. Answer: Y=6 Therefore, the correct answer is **Option C**.

da:2026:set1:main:q10.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 10
da:2026:set1:main:q10.question:
In the given figure, P, Q, and R are three points on a circle of radius $10\text{ cm}$ with $O$ as its center, $\overline{PQ} = \overline{RQ}$, and $\angle PQR = 45^\circ$. The figure is representative.

The area of the shaded region $PQRO$ is ______________ $\text{cm}^2$.
  1. $50$
  2. $25\sqrt{2}$
  3. $50\sqrt{2}$
  4. $100$

detailed_solution.markdown: Since $OP=OQ=OR=10$ (all radii) and $PQ=RQ$ (given), triangles $OPQ$ and $OQR$ are congruent (SSS: $OP=OR$, $OQ$ shared, $PQ=RQ$) — mirror images across line $OQ$. So the shaded region (quadrilateral $OPQR$) splits into two congruent triangles, and $\angle OQP=\angle OQR=\dfrac{45^\circ}2=22.5^\circ$ (splitting $\angle PQR$ equally by symmetry). In triangle $OPQ$ (isosceles, $OP=OQ$), the angles opposite these equal sides are also equal: $\angle OPQ=\angle OQP=22.5^\circ$. So $\angle POQ=180^\circ-22.5^\circ-22.5^\circ=135^\circ$. Area of triangle $OPQ=\dfrac12\cdot OP\cdot OQ\cdot\sin(\angle POQ)=\dfrac12(10)(10)\sin(135^\circ)=50\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt2}2=25\sqrt2$ Total shaded area $=2\times25\sqrt2=50\sqrt2$ Answer: $50\sqrt2$ Therefore, the correct answer is **Option C**.

da:2026:set1:main:q11.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 11
da:2026:set1:main:q11.question:
For a classification problem, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) has been used to reduce the dimensionality of a feature space from $100$ to $10$.
Which of the following options is true about the angle $\theta$ between the first and the tenth principal components?
  1. $\theta = 0^\circ$
  2. $\theta = 90^\circ$
  3. $90^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$
  4. $0 < \theta < 90^\circ$

detailed_solution.markdown: Principal Component Analysis produces principal components that are, by construction, mutually orthogonal (uncorrelated) directions — each new principal component is chosen to capture the remaining variance in a direction perpendicular to all previously chosen components. So the $1$st and $10$th principal components (like any two distinct principal components from the same PCA decomposition) are always exactly orthogonal to each other, i.e. the angle between them is $90^{\circ}$, regardless of how many dimensions were kept or discarded. Answer: θ=90° Therefore, the correct answer is **Option B**.

da:2026:set1:main:q12.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 12
da:2026:set1:main:q12.question:
Consider that you are training a classifier for a 10-class classification problem. Each input is represented as a 512-dimensional vector. There are $1000$ samples, out of which first $100$ will be used for testing. Let Leave-One-Out-Cross-Validation (LOOCV) be used for selection of the classifier model before testing.
Which of the following options is the correct number of validation splits that will be generated?
  1. $10$
  2. $512$
  3. $900$
  4. $1000$

detailed_solution.markdown: Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV) creates one validation split per training example: each split holds out exactly one sample for validation and trains on all the rest. The classifier model is being selected before testing, so LOOCV is applied only to the samples not reserved for testing. Out of $1000$ total samples, the first $100$ are held out for testing, leaving $1000-100=900$ samples available for model selection via LOOCV. LOOCV on $900$ samples generates exactly $900$ validation splits (one per sample). Answer: 900 Therefore, the correct answer is **Option C**.

da:2026:set1:main:q13.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 13
da:2026:set1:main:q13.question:
Which of the following algorithms is NOT an example of uninformed search?
  1. Breadth First Search
  2. Depth First Search
  3. A* Search
  4. Depth-limited Search

detailed_solution.markdown: Uninformed (blind) search algorithms explore the search space using no problem-specific knowledge beyond the raw structure of the graph/tree — they don't use any heuristic estimate of how close a state is to the goal. BFS, DFS, and Depth-limited Search are all classic examples of uninformed search, exploring purely based on the search tree's structure. A* Search, however, explicitly uses a heuristic function $h(n)$ (an estimate of the remaining cost to the goal) combined with the path cost so far, $f(n)=g(n)+h(n)$, to guide its search — making it an informed search algorithm, not uninformed. Answer: A* Search Therefore, the correct answer is **Option C**.

da:2026:set1:main:q14.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 14
da:2026:set1:main:q14.question:
Which of the following statements is NOT true? (The names of the predicates are intuitive.)
  1. $\forall x \forall y \; \text{Classmate}(x, y) \implies \text{Classmate}(y, x)$
  2. $\forall x \; \text{Likes}(x, \text{Icecream}) \implies \neg \exists x \; \neg \text{Likes}(x, \text{Icecream})$
  3. “Each king is a person” is equivalent to $\forall x \; \text{IsKing}(x) \land \text{IsPerson}(x)$
  4. “All humans are mortal” is equivalent to $\forall x \; \text{IsHuman}(x) \implies \text{IsMortal}(x)$

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - "Classmate is symmetric" ($\forall x\forall y\,\text{Classmate}(x,y)\Rightarrow\text{Classmate}(y,x)$): reasonably true given the intuitive meaning of "classmate." - "Everyone likes ice cream" phrased via a double negative ($\forall x\,\text{Likes}(x,\text{Icecream})\Rightarrow\neg\exists x\,\neg\text{Likes}(x,\text{Icecream})$): this is a valid logical equivalence (universal statement restated using negated existential), true. - "Each king is a person" as $\forall x\,\text{IsKing}(x)\wedge\text{IsPerson}(x)$: this is WRONG — using $\wedge$ (AND) here incorrectly asserts that everything in the domain is both a king and a person. The correct translation of "each king is a person" requires an implication: $\forall x\,\text{IsKing}(x)\Rightarrow\text{IsPerson}(x)$. Using AND instead of implication is a classic FOL translation error. - "All humans are mortal" via implication ($\forall x\,\text{IsHuman}(x)\Rightarrow\text{IsMortal}(x)$): this is the textbook-correct form, true. Answer: "Each king is a person" is equivalent to ∀x IsKing(x)∧IsPerson(x) (this statement is NOT true). Therefore, the correct answer is **Option C**.

da:2026:set1:main:q15.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 15
da:2026:set1:main:q15.question:
Consider that the quick sort algorithm is used to sort an array of $n$ distinct randomly ordered elements. In every call, the pivot is chosen as the first element of the current subarray.
Let $T(n)$ denote the expected time to sort the array. Assume that the time to partition is linear in the size of the current subarray.
Which of the following recurrence relations correctly represents $T(n)$ in this scenario?
  1. $T(n) = T(1) + T(n - 1) + O(n)$
  2. $T(n) = T\left(\frac{n}{4}\right) + T\left(\frac{3n}{4}\right) + O(n)$
  3. $T(n) = 2T\left(\frac{n}{2}\right) + O(n)$
  4. $T(n) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} [T(k) + T(n - k - 1)] + O(n)$

detailed_solution.markdown: With the pivot always chosen as the first element, and the input array being randomly ordered (so the pivot's rank is uniformly random among the $n$ elements of the current subarray), the pivot ends up at position $k$ (splitting into a left part of size $k$ and right part of size $n-k-1$) with equal probability $1/n$ for every $k=0,1,\ldots,n-1$. Averaging over all these equally likely splits gives the expected-case recurrence: $$T(n)=\dfrac1n\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\big[T(k)+T(n-k-1)\big]+O(n)$$ The other recurrences describe specific worst-case ($T(n)=T(1)+T(n-1)+O(n)$, when the pivot always lands at an extreme end) or idealized-balanced ($T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n)$) scenarios, not the true randomized average case. Answer: $T(n)=\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}[T(k)+T(n-k-1)]+O(n)$ Therefore, the correct answer is **Option D**.

da:2026:set1:main:q16.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 16
da:2026:set1:main:q16.question:
Consider the given Python program.
def append_to_lst(val, lst=[]):
    lst.append(val)
    return lst

print(append_to_lst(1))
print(append_to_lst(2))
print(append_to_lst(3, []))

Which of the following is the correct output of this program?
  1. [1]
    [2]
    [3]
  2. [1]
    [1, 2]
    [3]
  3. [1]
    [2]
    [1, 2, 3]
  4. [1]
    [1, 2]
    [1, 3]

detailed_solution.markdown: Python's mutable default argument gotcha: a default argument value (like $\text{lst=[]}$) is created once, when the function is defined, and is reused across all calls that don't explicitly supply their own argument for it — it does not get reset to a fresh empty list on each call. - $\text{append\_to\_lst(1)}$: no list passed, so it uses (and mutates) the shared default list: becomes $[1]$, printed as $[1]$. - $\text{append\_to\_lst(2)}$: again no list passed, so it reuses the same shared default list (still containing $1$ from before), appending $2$: becomes $[1,2]$, printed as $[1,2]$. - $\text{append\_to\_lst(3, [])}$: this call explicitly passes a brand-new, separate empty list, so it's unaffected by the shared default: becomes $[3]$, printed as $[3]$. Answer: [1], [1,2], [3] Therefore, the correct answer is **Option B**.

da:2026:set1:main:q17.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 17

Checking that no smaller (single-attribute) subset works confirms these three ($AD,ED,CD$) are exactly the minimal candidate keys — no others exist among the attribute combinations.   1. Slicing

da:2026:set1:main:q19.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 19
da:2026:set1:main:q19.question:
Let $M$ be a randomly chosen non-empty subset of $S = \{1, 2, 3, \dots, 2026\}$.
Which of the following is the probability that the product of all the elements of $M$ is even?
  1. $\frac{2^{1013}(2^{1013} - 1)}{2^{2026}}$
  2. $\frac{2^{1013}}{2^{2026}}$
  3. $\frac{2^{1013}(2^{1013} - 1)}{2^{2026} - 1}$
  4. $\frac{1}{2^{2026} - 1}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Among $\{1,\ldots,2026\}$, there are exactly $1013$ odd numbers and $1013$ even numbers. The product of all elements of $M$ is even unless every single chosen element is odd. Total non-empty subsets of $S$: $2^{2026}-1$. Non-empty subsets consisting only of odd numbers: $2^{1013}-1$ (choosing any non-empty subset of the $1013$ odd numbers). $P(\text{product odd})=\dfrac{2^{1013}-1}{2^{2026}-1}$ $P(\text{product even})=1-\dfrac{2^{1013}-1}{2^{2026}-1}=\dfrac{(2^{2026}-1)-(2^{1013}-1)}{2^{2026}-1}=\dfrac{2^{2026}-2^{1013}}{2^{2026}-1}=\dfrac{2^{1013}(2^{1013}-1)}{2^{2026}-1}$ Answer: $\dfrac{2^{1013}(2^{1013}-1)}{2^{2026}-1}$ Therefore, the correct answer is **Option C**.

da:2026:set1:main:q20.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 20
da:2026:set1:main:q20.question:
Suppose that a computer program provides a non-negative and integer-valued random solution to the equation $n_1 + n_2 + n_3 + n_4 = 20$.
Which of the following is the probability that all of $n_1, n_2, n_3, n_4$ in the provided solution are positive?
  1. $\frac{\binom{19}{3}}{\binom{23}{3}}$
  2. $\frac{\binom{20}{4}}{\binom{24}{4}}$
  3. $\frac{\binom{20}{3}}{\binom{23}{3}}$
  4. $\frac{\binom{19}{4}}{\binom{24}{4}}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Total non-negative integer solutions to $n_1+n_2+n_3+n_4=20$ (stars and bars): $\binom{20+4-1}{4-1}=\binom{23}{3}$ Solutions where every $n_i\ge1$ (all positive): substitute $m_i=n_i-1\ge0$, so $m_1+m_2+m_3+m_4=20-4=16$, giving $\binom{16+3}{3}=\binom{19}{3}$ such solutions. Assuming the "random solution" is chosen uniformly among all $\binom{23}{3}$ non-negative solutions, the probability that all $n_i$ turn out positive is: $\dfrac{\binom{19}{3}}{\binom{23}{3}}$ Answer: C(19,3)/C(23,3) Therefore, the correct answer is **Option A**.

da:2026:set1:main:q21.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 21
da:2026:set1:main:q21.question:
Let $M = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$ be a $2 \times 2$ matrix, where $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{5}$, and $I_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
Which of the following options is equal to $M^{2026}$?
  1. $M^2$
  2. $M$
  3. $M^{-1}$
  4. $I_2$

detailed_solution.markdown: $M$ is the standard $2\times2$ rotation matrix by angle $\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}5$. Rotation matrices compose by adding angles: $M^k$ is rotation by $k\theta=\dfrac{2\pi k}5$, and $M^k=I$ exactly when $k$ is a multiple of $5$ (a full $2\pi$ rotation, or multiple thereof). We want $M^{2026}$. Since $2025=5\times405$ is a multiple of $5$, $M^{2025}=I$, so: $M^{2026}=M^{2025}\cdot M=I\cdot M=M$ Answer: M Therefore, the correct answer is **Option B**.

da:2026:set1:main:q22.title: GATE DA 2026 | Question: 22
da:2026:set1:main:q22.question:
Consider a set $S_1 = \{x = (x_1, x_2, x_3)^T \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid x^T x \le 16\}$. Let $S_2$ be another set which is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with dimension two.
Which of the following gives the area of $S_1 \cap S_2$?
  1. $16\pi$
  2. $4\pi$
  3. $4\pi^2$
  4. $16\pi^2$

detailed_solution.markdown: $S_1=\{x\in\mathbb R^3\mid x^Tx\le16\}$ is a solid ball of radius $\sqrt{16}=4$ centered at the origin. $S_2$, being a $2$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb R^3$, is a plane passing through the origin. Intersecting a solid ball of radius $r$ (centered at the origin) with any plane through its center always yields a flat $2$D disk of the same radius $r$ (since the plane passes through the center, the cross-section is a full "great circle" disk, regardless of the plane's orientation). Let $f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 2$ be a function defined on $(-1, 3]$.
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
  1. $f(x)$ has exactly two roots in $[-0.9, 0]$.
  2. $f(x)$ has a local minimum at $x = 2$.
  3. $f(x)$ has a local maximum at $x = 0$.
  4. $f(x)$ has a root at $x = 1$.

detailed_solution.markdown: $f(x)=x^3-3x^2+2$ on $(-1,3]$. $f'(x)=3x^2-6x=3x(x-2)$, critical points at $x=0,2$. $f''(x)=6x-6$: $f''(0)=-6<0$ (local max at $0$), $f''(2)=6>0$ (local min at $2$). $f(0)=2$, $f(2)=-2$, and checking the included right endpoint $f(3)=27-27+2=2$ — the same value as $f(0)$! So the maximum value $2$ is attained at both $x=0$ and $x=3$, not just $x=0$ alone — that claim is false. $f(2)=-2$ remains the unique minimum (the excluded left endpoint $x=-1$ would give the same value $-2$, but since $-1$ isn't actually in the domain, it's never attained there) — so "minimum at $2$ only" is true. For roots in $[-0.9,0]$: $f$ is strictly increasing throughout this sub-interval (since $f'(x)=3x(x-2)>0$ for $x\in(-0.9,0)$, both factors negative), going from $f(-0.9)\approx-1.16$ up to $f(0)=2$ — crossing zero exactly once, not twice. That claim is false. Checking $f(1)=1-3+2=0$ — confirmed, $x=1$ is indeed a root. Answer: f has a minimum at 2 only; and f has a root at 1. Therefore, the correct option(s) are **B,D**.

For a given data set $\{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n\}$, where $n = 100$, it is known that $$\frac{1}{2000} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n (x_i - x_j)^2 = 99$$Let us denote $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i$.
The value of $$\frac{1}{99} \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2$$is __________ . (Answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: Expand the double sum using $x_i-x_j=(x_i-\bar x)-(x_j-\bar x)$: $\sum_i\sum_j(x_i-x_j)^2=n\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2-2\Big(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)\Big)\Big(\sum_j(x_j-\bar x)\Big)+n\sum_j(x_j-\bar x)^2$ Since $\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0$ always (by definition of the mean), the cross term vanishes, giving: $\sum_i\sum_j(x_i-x_j)^2=2n\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2$ So $\dfrac1{2000}\times2n\times SS=99$, where $SS=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$: $2(100)\,SS=198000\Rightarrow SS=\dfrac{198000}{200}=990$ $\dfrac1{99}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2=\dfrac{990}{99}=10$ Answer: 10 Therefore, the correct answer is **10**.

So $E[Y\mid X]=X^2$. $E[X]=0$ (symmetric uniform on $(-1,1)$). $\text{Cov}(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]=E\big[X\cdot E[Y\mid X]\big]-0=E[X\cdot X^2]=E[X^3]$ Since $X$ is symmetric about $0$, $E[X^3]=0$ (odd function integrated over a symmetric range). So $\text{Cov}(X,Y)=0$, and hence $\text{Correlation}(X,Y)=\dfrac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}=0$ (regardless of the exact value of $\sigma_Y$, since the numerator is zero). Let $A_{5 \times 5}$ be a matrix such that each of its elements follows $\text{Bernoulli}(p = 0.50)$ distribution independently.
The probability that the row-sum of the second row and the column-sum of the third column are both equal to $3$ is ________ . (Rounded off to two decimal places)

detailed_solution.markdown: Row $2$ and column $3$ share exactly one common cell (row $2$, column $3$), so these two sums aren't fully independent — condition on that shared cell's value $c\in\{0,1\}$ (each with probability $0.5$). Given $c$, the other $4$ cells of row $2$ must sum to $3-c$, and (independently) the other $4$ cells of column $3$ must also sum to $3-c$: $P(\text{both}\mid c)=\Big[\binom4{3-c}(0.5)^4\Big]^2$ For $c=0$ (need remaining $4$ to sum to $3$): $\binom43=4$, giving $[4/16]^2=0.0625$ For $c=1$ (need remaining $4$ to sum to $2$): $\binom42=6$, giving $[6/16]^2=0.140625$ Total $=0.5(0.0625)+0.5(0.140625)=0.03125+0.0703125\approx0.1016$ Answer: 0.10 Therefore, the correct answer is **0.08**.
